source: Introduction to AI - Teacher's Guide (AI Basics for Kids - 4-Week Sunday Class), 24-page edition, Oct 2026: each homework has a complete Version A and Version B.
scoring: Every homework is 100 points: multiple choice 30 (6 x 5, auto-marked) + short answer 10 (marked by the teacher) + task/upload 60 (marked by the teacher with a comment). Late work loses 10 points per day after 9pm, up to 50.
versions: Version A = James (younger, 11): more creative, more choice, shorter written parts. Version B = Peter (older, 12): more analysis, a stretch question. Both cover the same ideas.

lessons.title: What AI is and how it works
lessons.goal: Define AI correctly, explain how machine learning differs from normal programming, name the main milestones in AI history, and judge what a chatbot does well and badly.
lessons.key_terms: artificial intelligence, algorithm, machine learning, training data, model, prediction, narrow AI, general AI, supervised / unsupervised / reinforcement learning
theory: AI is computer systems doing tasks that normally need human intelligence: understanding language, recognising images, making decisions, creating content.
Normal programming: a person writes every rule. Machine learning: the computer is shown huge numbers of examples and works out the patterns itself.
Narrow AI does one kind of task (face unlock, translation, chatbots). General AI would match humans at almost everything; it does not exist yet.

History: 1950 Alan Turing asks "Can machines think?" (Turing Test); 1956 Dartmouth workshop names the field; 1997 Deep Blue beats Kasparov at chess; 2016 AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go; 2022 ChatGPT launches.
Progress sped up after 2010: more data from the internet, faster chips, better methods.

How machine learning works: training data -> training (finding patterns) -> model (the learned result) -> prediction (its best guess on something new). Example: a spam filter learning from millions of emails marked spam or not spam.
Three types: supervised (labelled examples), unsupervised (finds groups by itself), reinforcement (trial, reward and penalty).
A model is only as good as its data; bad or one-sided data gives bad or unfair results.
lessons.practical: AI audit of the apps they use (the AI feature, what it predicts, what data it learned from); live test of Claude's strengths and limits.

lessons.title: How chatbots work and how to use them well
lessons.goal: Explain how a chatbot produces an answer, why it sometimes makes things up, and how to write a prompt that gets a much better result.
lessons.key_terms: large language model (LLM), token, next-token prediction, parameters, training, fine-tuning, hallucination, knowledge cutoff, context window, diffusion model, prompt
theory: An LLM is a machine learning model trained on enormous amounts of text: books, websites, articles, code.

It reads and writes in tokens: small pieces of text, often part of a word (one English word is roughly 1-2 tokens). Its core skill is predicting the next token, again and again, to build a whole answer.
Parameters are billions of adjustable numbers tuned during training. Two stages: pre-training (patterns from huge text) and fine-tuning (people rate answers so it learns to be helpful).

Hallucination: it predicts what sounds right, not what is checked to be true. Knowledge cutoff: it only learned up to a certain date unless it can search the web. Tokens explain odd failures like counting letters. Context window: what it can hold in mind in one conversation.
Image generators use diffusion models: start from random noise and remove it step by step, guided by the text prompt.

Prompt framework: Role (who the AI should act as), Task (what exactly to do), Context (who it is for, background), Format (list, table, length). Follow-up prompts: ask to shorten, simplify or correct.
lessons.practical: Prompt structure (role, task, context, format); rewrite weak prompts ("help me with maths", "write a story", "make a study plan") and test them live on Claude.

lessons.title: Checking AI and staying safe
lessons.goal: Fact-check an AI answer properly, judge whether an image, video or voice may be AI-made, and know what personal information never goes into an AI app. Each student also picks a showcase topic.
lessons.key_terms: verification, reliable source, cross-checking, fabricated citation, deepfake, voice cloning, reverse image search, personal data, bias
theory: Treat an AI answer as a first draft, not a final fact, especially for names, numbers, dates and quotes. Cross-check with at least two reliable sources (official websites, established news outlets, encyclopedias, textbooks) and check the date.
AI can invent sources: book titles, links or quotes that do not exist. Always confirm a source is real.

A deepfake is AI-made or AI-edited video, audio or images showing a real person doing or saying something they never did. Voice cloning: a few seconds of voice can be enough, which scammers use in fake emergency calls.

Clues (odd hands or teeth, warped text, mismatched shadows, lips out of sync) are disappearing. Better checks: who posted it first, is a trusted outlet reporting it, what does a reverse image search show. Shocking content deserves more checking, not faster sharing.

Privacy: many AI apps store conversations and some use them to improve models. Never type passwords, home address, school name, phone numbers, ID or bank details, or private photos. Check app settings for chat history and data use.
Bias comes from training data that over- or under-represents groups. For school, AI is a tutor (explain, quiz, give feedback), not a ghostwriter.
lessons.practical: Test the prompt portfolios on Claude; fact-check Claude's answers with two reliable sources; choose showcase topics and write three main points.

lessons.title: AI and code, then the showcase
lessons.goal: Write and run a first Python program and present to the parents.
lessons.key_terms: code, programming language, algorithm, variable, input, output, condition (if/else), bug, AI coding assistant
theory: Code is exact instructions a computer follows, with no guessing. A programming language is how we write them. Python is the most popular language for AI because it is readable and has strong AI libraries.

An algorithm is a step-by-step method to solve a problem. Building blocks: variables (storing information), input and output (asking and showing), conditions (if this, do that; otherwise, do something else).

AI coding assistants are LLMs trained on huge amounts of public code, using the same next-token prediction. They write and explain code fast, but the code can contain bugs, so a programmer must read, test and understand it.
Careers: machine learning engineer, data scientist, AI researcher, AI safety researcher, software developer. Base skills: maths, programming, clear writing, learning to check your work.
lessons.practical: A rule-based mini chatbot in Python (input, variables, if/elif/else), then add at least three new rules each; contrast with Claude, which can answer almost anything.
